text.title: API Gateway Patterns & Technology Selection Core Rules
text.summary: Testable rules every api-gateway-patterns application MUST enforce, plus a skip-this-methodology fallback. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: Use simple routing when the architecture has a direct mapping between client requests and backend services with minimal transformation needed and a single client type or uniform client needs.
rule.rationale: Simple routing avoids operational overhead of BFF or aggregation patterns. Adding patterns prematurely creates maintenance burden without benefit.

rule.statement: Use BFF when different clients have vastly different data needs, mobile needs optimized payloads, third-party integrations require different contracts, or different security requirements exist per client type.
rule.rationale: A single gateway serving all clients tends to accumulate client-specific logic and becomes a bottleneck; BFF pushes that complexity to per-client surfaces owned by the teams that know those clients.

rule.statement: Use aggregation when reducing client-side complexity is a primary goal, when minimizing network round trips matters (mobile, low-bandwidth), or when creating composite API views from independently deployed services.
rule.rationale: Without aggregation, clients make N parallel requests; mobile clients on slow links feel latency multiplied by the number of services. Aggregation at the gateway trades gateway complexity for client simplicity.

rule.statement: Use edge+mesh when services require mutual TLS between them, when fine-grained traffic management between services is needed, or when a zero-trust security model is required. Do NOT use a service mesh for a simple two-tier app — the operational overhead is substantial.
rule.rationale: The mesh handles east-west (service-to-service) while the gateway handles north-south (client-to-gateway). Combining them avoids duplicating concerns at both layers.

rule.statement: Every gateway selection MUST document at least one rejected alternative with a one-sentence reason. Selections without rejected alternatives are blocked.
rule.rationale: Without rejected alternatives the ADR is decision laundering and provides no audit value.

rule.statement: The selected gateway MUST be stateless: it operates only on request headers, path and auth tokens. Auth state lives in tokens (JWT, mTLS certs, signed cookies); rate-limit counters live in shared Redis, never in gateway process memory. Plugins (Lua, JS, WASM) are reserved for auth, rate-limit, request-tracing and CORS — any aggregation or transformation belongs in a BFF service.
rule.rationale: Stateless gateways scale horizontally and survive restarts. Business logic in plugins creates a second monolith owned by the platform team, invisible to domain developers and gated by a separate release cycle.

rule.statement: Rate limiting MUST be per-consumer (API key, authenticated user id) or per-plan, never per source IP when the gateway sits behind a CDN or load balancer. Behind a CDN, rate-limit on the client IP carried in X-Forwarded-For or on the authenticated subject, never on the CDN's IP.
rule.rationale: Behind a proxy all traffic arrives from a small IP set, so one consumer exhausts the bucket for everyone. Consumer-scoped limiting is correct regardless of network topology and is attributable.

rule.statement: Every inbound request MUST carry a unique X-Request-ID, generated at ingress when absent ($request_id in nginx, correlation-id plugin in Kong), propagated to every downstream service, and emitted in the structured logs of every hop.
rule.rationale: Correlation ids are the only reliable way to reconstruct a failed request across services; timestamp matching is unreliable under concurrent traffic. Cost is one header assignment at the edge.

rule.statement: Timeouts MUST descend: upstream < gateway < client, with at least 50% headroom at each step (for example 2s upstream, 5s gateway, 10s client). A gateway timeout greater than or equal to the client timeout is a defect.
rule.rationale: If the client aborts first it loses the gateway's 504 and may retry while the gateway is still retrying upstream — cascading load and thundering herd. A short gateway timeout fails fast with a clear error the client can handle.

rule.statement: Circuit breakers MUST be configured per upstream service, never globally. One failing upstream returns 503 for its own routes only while healthy routes keep serving. Implement with Kong request-termination or Envoy outlier_detection.
rule.rationale: A global breaker converts one slow service into a total outage, and without per-service isolation a slow upstream exhausts the gateway's connection pool and degrades every route.

rule.statement: Gateway configuration MUST be versioned in git and applied by CI (deck for Kong, Terraform for AWS API Gateway, Argo CD/Flux for Kubernetes). Route or plugin changes made through a web UI or a hand-run reload without a matching PR are rejected. nginx is for expert operators only — it has no dynamic reload without OpenResty; Envoy implies a mesh deployment.
rule.rationale: UI changes are unversioned, unreviewed and unreproducible, with no rollback path; a mis-click takes down all traffic. Declarative config makes the diff reviewable and replayable in a new environment.

rule.statement: When Kong is selected, commit to DB mode (PostgreSQL, live updates, multiple instances in sync, needed above ~10k req/s) or DB-less mode (config from file/ConfigMap, static, faster) and do not switch mid-flight.
rule.rationale: The two modes have different update semantics; migrating between them while serving traffic loses gateway state.

rule.statement: A BFF MUST fan out to upstreams in parallel (asyncio.gather, Promise.all, goroutines) with a per-service timeout rather than one global timeout, and MUST degrade partially — a timed-out upstream yields null or an empty list in the composed response instead of failing the whole request. A BFF MUST NOT cache; caching belongs at the gateway.
rule.rationale: Serial fan-out multiplies latency and a global timeout lets one slow upstream block the composition. Caching at the gateway saves both the aggregation and the upstream cost, which caching inside the BFF does not.

rule.statement: If any Applies-If precondition fails OR any Skip-If condition triggers, do NOT apply this methodology. Emit a skip-record naming the failed precondition / triggered skip, and route the task to the correct methodology (or none).
rule.rationale: Methodology hygiene: mis-application produces worse artefacts than no methodology because downstream consumers trust the schema; the skip-record makes non-application traceable.
